passages.text: Paired Exome-Based Comprehensive Genomic Profiling and Germline Genetic Testing for Unselected Patients With Colorectal Cancer in a Multicenter Prospective Study
Background and Aims

Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) for tumors and germline genetic testing (GGT) inform precision therapy and clinical management of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), and evidence is growing in support of universal paired CGP-GGT patient testing. <sentence_start/>However, the utility of combining CGP and GGT for early-stage CRC (ESC) and early-onset CRC (EOC) is unclear.
Methods

We performed a prospective, multisite study featuring GGT using an 80+ gene next-generation sequencing platform and exome-based CGP among CRC patients (unselected for age, stage, family history) receiving care at Mayo Clinic Cancer Centers between April 1, 2018, and March 31, 2020.
Results

A total of 150 CRC patients had GGT and exome-based CGP performed. <sentence_start/>ESC patients had an enrichment of high microsatellite instability and high tumor mutation burden. <sentence_start/>High microsatellite instability was also enriched in those with smoking history, and in tumors with mutated <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic>, homologous recombination deficiency, or at least 1 variant in the rat sarcoma virus pathway. <sentence_start/>Moreover, patients with smoking history were enriched in <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> and other Tier 1 or 2 variants overall. <sentence_start/>Sixteen percent of patients harbored a pathogenic germline variant, most frequent being in Lynch syndrome genes. <sentence_start/>Paired GGT and CGP testing had high rates of clinically significant findings (≈70%) with the most frequent being high tumor mutation burden status. <sentence_start/>Pathway and mutational signature analysis revealed frequent CGP mutations in DNA repair and cell cycle pathways.
Conclusion

These data suggest that universal, combined GGT-CGP increases clinical utility for EOC and ESC patients. <sentence_start/>This is key for EOC patients who tend to experience poorer outcomes. <sentence_start/>CGP-GGT expedites germline resolution for tumor mutations in hereditary cancer genes, reducing delays and facilitating identification of relevant therapies, clinical trials, and management recommendations.
Introduction

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer worldwide, accounting for about 10% of all cancer cases, and is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths.<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38572751" doi="10.3322/caac.21834" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In 2022, there were an estimated 1,926,118 new cases and 903,859 deaths of CRC worldwide.<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38572751" doi="10.3322/caac.21834" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In the United States, in 2024, there were an estimated 152,810 new cases and 53,010 deaths.<citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3322/caac.21824" pmid="38230825" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation>

Risk factors for developing CRC include age, family and personal history of colon or related cancers, and lifestyle factors.<citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3322/caac.21824" pmid="38230825" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35090605" doi="10.1016/S2468-1253(21)00426-X" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>About 15% of patients with CRC are carriers of pathogenic germline variants (PGVs), most in moderate- and high-penetrance cancer susceptibility genes.<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33857637" doi="10.1016/j.cgh.2021.04.013" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation>

Early-onset CRC (EOC) is on the rise.<citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35090605" doi="10.1016/S2468-1253(21)00426-X" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>EOC is usually defined as a patient that develops CRC before 50 years old.<citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35090605" doi="10.1016/S2468-1253(21)00426-X" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The definition of the age of EOC is based on historical screening indications and could change in face of new screening guidelines recommendations (ie, 45 years old).<citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35090605" doi="10.1016/S2468-1253(21)00426-X" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Multiple factors are related to increased incidence of CRC in young patients worldwide, which would be related to PGVs, polygenic and familial risk, environmental exposures (exposome), and even a high-risk microbiota related to Western diets.<citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35090605" doi="10.1016/S2468-1253(21)00426-X" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation>

Paired germline and somatic analysis in patients with CRC are valuable to not only identify the full scope of genomic alterations but also as a strategy to maximize actionable treatment for precision medicine initiatives and genetic counseling, in both late-onset and EOC.<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35218578" doi="10.1002/jgc4.1567" pmcid="PMC9544955" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation>

However, barriers have been identified with implementation of paired universal testing, including lack of consensus on how to integrate the findings, lack of guidelines, insurance coverage, concern about potentially widening health inequities, potential liability or clinician hesitancy, and the real-world actionability of the findings.<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35218578" doi="10.1002/jgc4.1567" pmcid="PMC9544955" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30130624" doi="10.1016/j.cgh.2018.08.038" pmcid="PMC6866232" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33126242" doi="10.1001/jamaoncol.2020.6252" pmcid="PMC7600058" count="1">7</citation>

With the objective of evaluating the impact of universal testing for late and EOC (<45 y/o), prospective exome-based comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) on tumor samples and germline genetic testing (GGT) were performed for a cohort of patients with CRC.
Materials and Methods
Colorectal Cancer Cohort

A prospective unselected CRC patient cohort (n = 150) of patients receiving care at Mayo Clinic Cancer Centers in Rochester, Minnesota; Jacksonville, Florida; and Phoenix, Arizona, and in a community oncology practice (Mayo Clinic Health System, Eau Claire, Wisconsin), between April 1, 2018, and March 31, 2020, for the Interrogating Cancer Etiology Using Proactive Genetic Testing program was assessed by paired GGT and CGP.<citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33126242" doi="10.1001/jamaoncol.2020.6252" pmcid="PMC7600058" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>CGP included assessment of sequence variants, amplifications, microsatellite instability (MSI) and tumor mutation burden (TMB). <sentence_start/>The study methodology for Interrogating Cancer Etiology Using Proactive Genetic Testing is briefly described below, and additional details are available in Samadder et al.<citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33126242" doi="10.1001/jamaoncol.2020.6252" pmcid="PMC7600058" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation> Research coordinators completed patient recruitment using central lists of daily oncology clinic visits. <sentence_start/>Patients were unselected for race/ethnicity, disease stage, family or personal history of cancer, age at disease onset, and other parameters. <sentence_start/>All patients viewed a standardized pretest genetics education video, were offered pre-test genetic counseling, and provided written informed consent. <sentence_start/>Data were deidentified to all except study investigators. <sentence_start/>Detailed clinicopathological features were collected from medical records, self-administered electronic questionnaires, and an electronic family cancer pedigree tool (Cancer Gene Connect). <sentence_start/>This study was approved by the Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board (19-010300). <sentence_start/>EOC was defined as onset of CRC <45 years of age. <sentence_start/>Early-stage CRC (ESC) was defined as stages 0-III.
DNA Isolation and Sequencing

Specimens underwent clinical testing at Invitae (now part of LabCorp San Francisco, CA), a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments-certified, New York state-certified and College of American Pathology-accredited genetic diagnostics laboratory. <sentence_start/>Genomic DNA for GGT was isolated from whole blood and saliva using a Hamilton STAR (Hamilton Company, Reno, NV) and the Omega Bio-tek HDQ DNA extraction kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA). <sentence_start/>Next-generation sequencing (NGS) enriched targeted regions using a hybridization-based protocol and sequenced using Illumina technology (Illumina; La Jolla, CA). <sentence_start/>Hybridization capture probes targeted 80 or more genes, featuring full-gene sequencing (including coding exons, 20 base pairs of adjacent intronic sequencing on either side of the coding exons and select noncoding variants) and deletion-duplication analysis for single nucleotide variants (SNVs), small insertion/deletions (indels), copy number variants (CNVs), and splice site variants. <sentence_start/>All targeted regions were sequenced with ≥50x depth or were supplemented with additional analysis.<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34007000" doi="10.1038/s41436-021-01187-w" pmcid="PMC8460443" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Confirmation of the presence and location of reportable variants is performed as needed based on stringent criteria using one of several validated orthogonal approaches.<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30610921" doi="10.1016/j.jmoldx.2018.10.009" pmcid="PMC6629256" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation>

DNA was extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue for CGP using the DNA formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded isolation system (Promega) on the automated King Fisher Flex platform (Thermo Fisher). <sentence_start/>NGS libraries of the tumor DNA were generated using the DNA Library Prep Kit with Fragmentation (Watchmaker Genomics; Boulder, CO) and underwent exome capture using custom probes (targeting coding exons, 10 base pairs of adjacent intronic sequencing on either side of the coding exons and select noncoding variants) with the Fast Hybridization and Wash Kit with Amplification Mix (Twist Bioscience; San Francisco, CA). <sentence_start/>The sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq6000 using 2 × 150 reads, to at least 250x mean coverage (range 260-1189x).
Germline Specimen Processing and Review

Full gene sequencing, deletion/duplication analysis, and variant interpretation using an NGS panel of 80+ genes on the Invitae Multi-Cancer panel was offered at no cost as previously described.<citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33126242" doi="10.1001/jamaoncol.2020.6252" pmcid="PMC7600058" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>NGS reads were aligned to the reference human genome sequence hg19 (GRCh37) using NoVo align (NoVo craft Technologies; Selangor, Malaysia). <sentence_start/>Small indels and SNVs were analyzed using the Genome Analysis Toolkit Unified Genotyper,<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20644199" doi="10.1101/gr.107524.110" pmcid="PMC2928508" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation> Freebayes,<citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation> and Coalgen (unpublished). <sentence_start/>CNV calls were performed using the in-house algorithm, CNVitae.<citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Large structural variants were detected using split-read analysis as described previously.<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2164-12-184" pmcid="PMC3088570" pmid="21486468" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>More details regarding workflow are described previously.<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34007000" doi="10.1038/s41436-021-01187-w" pmcid="PMC8460443" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30610921" doi="10.1016/j.jmoldx.2018.10.009" pmcid="PMC6629256" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The technique was used at all <italic toggle="yes">loci</italic>, allowing for the detection of certain structural variants that can evade both read-depth analysis (those with breakpoints within a small assay target) and indel detection (large structural variants or with breakpoints outside of targeted regions). <sentence_start/>Variants were assessed using a refined version of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics criteria (Sherloc).<citation rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28492532" doi="10.1038/gim.2017.37" pmcid="PMC5632818" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Alterations were defined as on-target when they occurred in genes associated with hereditary cancer syndrome with an associated increased risk for CRC; while alterations were considered as off-target when they occurred in hereditary cancer risk syndrome genes not commonly associated with an increased risk for CRC.
Tumor Specimen Processing and Review

Tumor sequencing FASTQs were preprocessed by fastp (v0.23.4)<citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30423086" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/bty560" pmcid="PMC6129281" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation> and were aligned to the hg19 human genome by BWA (v0.7.17)<citation rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19451168" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btp324" pmcid="PMC2705234" count="1"><sup>16</sup></citation> and Abra2 (v2.2).<citation rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30649250" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btz033" pmcid="PMC6735753" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>PCR duplicates were removed by Picard (v3.1.1) ( ). <sentence_start/>SNVs and Indels were detected by Vardict (v1.8.3)<citation rid="bib18" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27060149" doi="10.1093/nar/gkw227" pmcid="PMC4914105" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> and MUTECT2 (GATK4 v.4.2.0.0).<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Variants were annotated using Nirvana Annotator (v0.3).<citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Variants were assessed according to Association of American Pathology/American Society of Clinical Oncology/College of American Pathology guidelines<citation rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmoldx.2016.10.002" pmcid="PMC5707196" pmid="27993330" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation> with review limited to variants occurring in 191 clinically significant cancer-associated genes. <sentence_start/>MSI was assessed utilizing a custom tool, AbsoluteMSI (v0.1) (unpublished) and reported as microsatellite stable (MSS) or unstable (high microsatellite instability [MSI-H]). <sentence_start/>CNV profile was detected by PureCN (v0.3)<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27999612" doi="10.1186/s13029-016-0060-z" pmcid="PMC5157099" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> and manually reviewed for gene level amplifications for select clinically significant genes (<italic toggle="yes">ERBB2, FGFR1-3, CCND1, CCNDE, MYC</italic>) as well as genes mutated in the germline or somatic sample in which a possible second hit is potentially indicated. <sentence_start/>Nonsynonymous exonic variants that exhibited a high posterior probability of being somatic after assessment by somatic-germline-zygosity algorithm were utilized to calculate TMB.<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005965" pmcid="PMC5832436" pmid="29415044" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Somatic findings were further assessed for clinical significance based on treatment associations in CRC, treatment associations in other solid tumors, prognostic implications for CRC, and clinical trial eligibility. <sentence_start/>Tumor samples were assessed for quality control metrics based on variant-type based thresholds. <sentence_start/>All samples passed SNV/small-indel variant quality control (QC) while 13 failed MSI QC and 16 failed TMB QC; variant types failing QC were excluded from analysis. <sentence_start/>On-target variations were defined as changes in the DNA that occurred at the specific and intended location of genetic locus; off-target variations were variations that occurred at unintended locations of the genome. <sentence_start/>Tier 1 and tier 2 variations were defined as clinical and potential meaningful variants, related to significance, actionability, and evidence of impact of patient care.
Statistical Assessments and Figure Generation

Patient demographics and genetic results were compiled and assessed in R ( ) to produce summary, Pearson Chi-squared test, Fisher exact test, figures, and additional assessments.<citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Oncoprinter was utilized for the co-occurrence assessment.<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30341162" doi="10.1101/gr.239244.118" pmcid="PMC6211645" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Pathway analysis was completed using Reactome GSA.<citation rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32907876" doi="10.1074/mcp.TIR120.002155" pmcid="PMC7710148" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Mutational signatures were assessed with mut Signatures R package.<citation rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33106540" doi="10.1038/s41598-020-75062-0" pmcid="PMC7589488" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation>
Results
Cohort Characteristics

General patient demographics and disease characteristics are shown in Table. <sentence_start/>Forty-two percent (63/150) of patients were female and 84.0% (126/150) were non-Hispanic White. <sentence_start/>EOC was present in 19.3% (29/150) of patients. <sentence_start/>Sixty-two percent (18/29) of patients with EOC were diagnosed at an early stage (0 to III). <sentence_start/>Late-stage disease was diagnosed with 30.0% (45/150) of patients. <sentence_start/>The most common tumor location was rectal in 43.3% (65/150) of patients, and surgical resection was performed in 91.3% (137/150) of cases. <sentence_start/>Comorbidities included a history of smoking in 39.3% (59/150), obesity in 37.3% (56/150), hypertension in 38.0% (57/150), and diabetes in 8.0% (12/150) of patients. <sentence_start/>A family history of cancer was reported in 60.0% of patients (90/150), and a family history of gastrointestinal cancers was reported in 24.7% (37/150) of patients.
Germline Analysis

For the 150 CRC patients included in this study, PGVs were detected in 24/150 patients (16.0%), 58 (38.7%) had uncertain results, and 68 (45.3%) had negative results. <sentence_start/>Of PGV results, 45.8% (n = 11) were on-target and 54.2% (n = 13) were off-target. <sentence_start/>The most common on-target PGVs were in Lynch syndrome genes (<italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic>, n = 4; <italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>, n = 1; <italic toggle="yes">MSH3</italic>, n = 1). <sentence_start/>Logistic regression modeling showed family history of gastrointestinal cancers (odds ratio [OR] = 2.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.03-6.53, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .039) and obesity (OR = 0.12, 95% CI = 0.02-0.44, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .006) were associated with having a PGV result. <sentence_start/>Fourteen cases were considered to have clinically significant germline findings with defined clinical management guidelines (9.3%). <sentence_start/>Of these, 28.6% (4/14) had precision therapy approved in another tumor type (ie, Poly Adenosine Diphosphate Ribose Polymerase inhibitors), and 64.3% (9/14) with potential clinical trials eligibility (Supplementary Table 1).
Somatic Analysis
Variant analysis

Of the 150 patients, 132 (88.0%) had somatic findings of established or potential clinical significance (Tier 1/Tier 2), including detection of 707 total Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants (Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Patients had a median of 4 Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants (Figure 1C) with missense and loss of function variants, particularly nonsense and frameshift deletions (Figure 1B) being the most common type of alterations. <sentence_start/>By logistic regression, colon cancers were significantly associated with a lower likelihood of somatic findings when compared to rectal cancers (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.39, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .001). <sentence_start/>The most frequent somatic findings were <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> loss of function variants and <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> hotspot missense variants (Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Half of patients with <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> variants harbored more than 1 variant. <sentence_start/>Additionally, the <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> c.835-8A>G splice variant was detected in 4.7% (n = 7) of patients (Supplementary Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Multiple variants were found to be recurrent in the cohort including <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> c.35G>T (p. Gly12Val) and c.38G>A (p. Gly13Asp), <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> c.1799T>A (p. Val600Glu), <italic toggle="yes">RNF43</italic> c.1976del (p. Gly659ValfsTer41), and <italic toggle="yes">TCF7L2</italic> c.1385dup (p. Cys463ValfsTer8) (Supplementary Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Additionally, BRAF mutations were found to be statistically associated with smoking history (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .027). <sentence_start/>The somatic mutational spectrum did not statistically differ between EOC and typical onset CRC. <sentence_start/>While not statistically significant, select gene variants were observed at lower rates in the EOC patients, including <italic toggle="yes">BRAF, RNF43, MSH3, BLM, AMER1, ATM</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">CREBBP</italic>. <sentence_start/>Variants of established significance were concentrated in <italic toggle="yes">KRAS, BRAF</italic>, and mismatch repair (MMR) genes (<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MSH3</italic>). <sentence_start/>In 77 patients (51.3%), 129 Tier 1/2 variants were detected in hereditary cancer syndrome associated genes (n = 26) at allele frequencies of 30.0%-70.0%, suggesting possible germline origin. <sentence_start/>Of those, 18/129 (14.0%) were confirmed to be germline variants. <sentence_start/>When considering only genes where variants have high germline likelihood (<italic toggle="yes">BLM, MSH6, CHEK2, MSH2, AXIN2, MLH1, BARD1, ATM, BRCA2, RAD51D, BRCA1, MSH3, FLCN, SDHD, BRIP1, MUTYH, SDHA</italic>), when detected somatically, 16/34 (47.1%) were confirmed to be germline variants.<sentence_start/>Figure 1

Summary of somatic findings in patients with positive findings. <sentence_start/>For patients with positive somatic findings (n = 132), (A) details the most frequently altered genes in the cohort, including the mean variant allele frequency (VAF) and the proportion of each variant type identified, as well as the proportion of transitions and transversions seen in each patient. <sentence_start/>Each column in the graph represents a single patient. <sentence_start/>In (B), variant types and functional classification of variants across the cohort are summarized. <sentence_start/>In (C), the per sample distribution of variant count and type is shown.
Tumor Mutation Burden/Microsatellite Instability

TMB ranged from 0.5 to 245.9 mutations/megabase (muts/Mb) with a mean of 15.5 muts/Mb. <sentence_start/>Twenty-seven samples (18.0%) had a TMB ≥10 muts/Mb (high tumor mutation burden [TMB-H]). <sentence_start/>Characterization of MSI indicated that 12/150 (8.0%) tumors exhibited MSI-H. Most were MSS (n = 144, 96.0%) profile and had a TMB <10 muts/Mb (Supplementary Figures 2 and 3). <sentence_start/>MSI-H status was significantly associated with TMB-H (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 1.566e-09). <sentence_start/>Additionally, assessment indicated an enrichment of MSI-H status in ESC patients (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .018), patients with smoking history (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .012), in tumors with mutated <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 2.837E-4) and with at least 1 mutation in <italic toggle="yes">BRAF/KRAS/NRAS</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .013). <sentence_start/>TMB-H was also enriched in ESC patients, particularly patients with stage II CRC (Supplementary Figure 2 and Supplementary Table 2).
Clinical Significance of Somatic Findings

Of 150 patients, 88 (58.7%) had potentially clinically significant variants detected in at least 1 of 5 categories across 52 genes (Figure 2). <sentence_start/>This included 95 variants with a Tier 1 therapeutic sensitivity or resistance implication in CRC, 86 variants with a Tier 2 therapeutic sensitivity or resistance implication in CRC, 130 variants with a therapeutic sensitivity in another solid tumor type, 52 variants with a prognostic implication in CRC, and 228 with clinical trial associations for CRC or a solid tumor (591 total associations across 289 variants). <sentence_start/>Of 289 variants detected across 52 genes, the most frequently detected were variants in <italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic> (51), <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic> (21), <italic toggle="yes">FBXW7</italic> (18), <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> (15), <italic toggle="yes">PTEN</italic> (15), and <italic toggle="yes">RNF43</italic> (15). <sentence_start/>Twenty-seven of the 88 cases with somatic findings were TMB-H with 12 (44.4%) of those patients also characterized as MSI-H. Both TMB-H and MSI-H status are eligible for immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and confer eligibility for additional clinical trials. <sentence_start/>For 5/88 cases, TMB-H status was the only clinically significant finding.<sentence_start/>Figure 2
Clinically significant types of somatic variants. <sentence_start/>In the figure, variants are classified accordingly with actionability, clinical trials available, and prognostic implications.
Combined Germline and Somatic

Ten percent (15/150) of patients were negative for both germline and somatic findings of established or potential clinical significance. <sentence_start/>In total 76.0% (114/150) had either a GGT (n = 3) or CGP (n = 111) clinically significant findings, while 14.0% (21/150) cases had both CGP and GGT clinically significant findings. <sentence_start/>Among EOC patients (n = 29), 6 (20.7%) had PGVs, in which all patients had additional Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants, while 20 (70.0%) only had somatic Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants, and 3 (10.3%) were negative for PGVs or somatic variants of clinical significance. <sentence_start/>Among ESC patients (n = 105), 18 (17.1%) had PGVs in which 17/18 (94.4%) had additional somatic Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants, 76 (72.4%) only had somatic Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants, and 11 (10.5%) had both (Figure 3). <sentence_start/>Combined GGT and CGP testing significantly increased clinically significant findings over GGT alone (74.0%), but only modestly over somatic testing alone (2.7%) (Figure 4). <sentence_start/>These findings were similar when subsetting for ESC (increased utility over GGT alone: 72.4%, increased utility over somatic testing alone: 2.9%) and EOC increased utility over GGT alone: 69.0%, increased utility over somatic testing alone: 6.9%).Figure 3
Proportion of germline and somatic findings in cohort. <sentence_start/>Germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic (LP/P) findings are further detailed as on or off target for colorectal cancer.
Figure 4

Clinical utility of combined germline and somatic testing. <sentence_start/>Frequency of patients with somatic and germline testing, broken down by age of onset and stage of patients. <sentence_start/>The increased utility of the CGP-GGT testing is indicated as well. <sentence_start/>Early-stage considered localized disease (stages 0-3).
Pathway Analysis

Pathway analysis of CGP findings indicated an enrichment of mutations in DNA repair pathways (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 6.420 E<sup>−10</sup>; FDR = 1.520 E<sup>−07</sup>) and the cell cycle (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 1.230 E<sup>−07</sup>; FDR:1.330 E<sup>−05</sup>). <sentence_start/>Alterations were frequent in the double strand break response (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 1.650 E<sup>−06</sup>; FDR: 1.520 E<sup>−04</sup>); largely focused on the homologous recombination repair (HRR) pathway (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 3.770 E<sup>−14</sup>-1.530 E<sup>−08</sup>; FDR: 1.570 E<sup>−11</sup>-2.540 E<sup>−06</sup>). <sentence_start/>Alterations associated with the <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> DNA damage pathway were also significantly enriched (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 1.110 E<sup>−16</sup>; FDR: 1.850 E<sup>−13</sup>). <sentence_start/>Additionally, oncogenic signaling in the rat sarcoma virus/rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 1.710 E<sup>−9</sup>-2.770 E<sup>−6</sup>; FDR: 3.140 E<sup>−7</sup>-2.410 E<sup>−4</sup>) and PI3K pathways (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 1.710 E<sup>−9</sup>-3.990 E<sup>−6</sup>; FDR: 3.140 E<sup>−7</sup>-3.050 E<sup>−4</sup>) were frequently altered in the cohort. <sentence_start/>No difference was observed in pathway enrichment between early and late disease onset (Supplementary Tables 3-5; Figure 5).Figure 5

Pathway enrichment analysis of cohort. <sentence_start/>Figure highlights the pathways enriched in mutations in the cohort, with analysis highlighting an abundance of genes within the cell cycle and DNA damage pathways being altered in the dataset.

Mutations in 20 genes were found to significantly co-occur with another gene within the dataset; no statistically significant mutually exclusive relationships were identified. <sentence_start/>Previously unreported co-occurrence relationships identified in the cohort included <italic toggle="yes">ATM-B2M, MSH6-B2M, RNF43-CDK12</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=<.001) (Supplementary Table 3).
Mutational Signature Analysis

Mutational signature analysis identified 3 main functional mutational signatures (<italic toggle="yes">POLE</italic>, defective MMR [dMMR], and defective homologous recombination deficiency [HRD]) (Supplementary Table 4). <sentence_start/>This analysis highlighted the driving effect of mutations within the HRR, MMR and POLE pathways. <sentence_start/>Two patients with EOC exhibited <italic toggle="yes">POLE</italic> mutation signatures (SBS 10a and 10b) and had <italic toggle="yes">POLE</italic> hotspot mutations. <sentence_start/>Sequencing identified a somatic <italic toggle="yes">POLE</italic> c.857C>G p. Pro286Arg mutation in both patients at allele frequencies of 24.5% and 25.1%, respectively. <sentence_start/>One patient was diagnosed with stage II colon cancer at age 44 years and had a TMB value of 245.9 muts/Mb, indicating hypermutator status. <sentence_start/>Another patient was diagnosed with stage III rectal cancer at age 39 years. <sentence_start/>The patient had a family history of cancer but not gastrointestinal cancer. <sentence_start/>While the sample failed TMB QC and therefore TMB was not reported, the patient did exhibit a high number of variants post-filtering for variant review indicating that the patient may have had a high TMB.

A 65-year-old rectal cancer patient exhibited a strong HRD mutational signature (SBS 3). <sentence_start/>The results of CGP indicated that the tumor was MSS and had a high TMB of 15.7; however, no HRD pathway mutations were detected.

Additionally, 12 patients were found to exhibit dMMR mutational signatures. <sentence_start/>Of these, 4 (33.3%) patients had oncogenic dMMR mutations identified. <sentence_start/>Three of the 4 had both single-base substitutions (SBS) signature 6 and 26 identified, which are associated with dMMR and MSI. <sentence_start/>Additionally, all had high TMB rates and were MSI-H. A patient diagnosed with stage III rectal cancer at age 27 years had a heterozygous germline <italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic> c.187del (p. Gly62_Val63insTer) pathogenic variant, while the other 3 patients had somatic variants in dMMR genes. <sentence_start/>Overall, the data indicate that these 4 tumors were driven by dMMR mutations. <sentence_start/>Eight tumors with dMMR mutational signatures (SBS signature 26, with another case also exhibiting signature 6) did not have GGT or CGP MMR gene variants identified. <sentence_start/>These 8 samples had low TMB and were MSS. <sentence_start/>These patients were all diagnosed at ≤ 62 years old, including 2 EOC cases that were negative for any PGVs. <sentence_start/>Additionally, 11 samples were positive for MMR variants, but the dMMR mutational signature was not detected. <sentence_start/>In these 11 cases, TMB was high in 63.6% (n = 7) cases.
Disease-Specific Outcomes

Comparing median overall survival, neither any statistical difference was identified between patients with or without PGVs (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .630) nor in patients with or without somatic variants (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .600) (Supplementary Figures 4 and 5). <sentence_start/>For patients with resectable disease, recurrence-free survival was also not associated with germline or somatic alterations (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .110 and <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .490), respectively (Supplementary Figures 6 and 7).
Discussion

The combination of exome-based CGP with comprehensive GGT realized in this study, in a prospective multicenter cohort of patients, provided valuable insights into the impact of paired genomic profiling in unselected patients with CRC. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, with the integration of clinical demographics, we identified associations with molecular characteristics including TMB-H with ESC. <sentence_start/>Combining GGT and CGP increased the likelihood of identifying clinically significant findings. <sentence_start/>Finally, exome CGP analysis identified enrichment of mutations in DNA repair and cell cycle pathways in the overall cohort.

In this cohort of unselected patients with CRC, 16.0% of the patients harbored PGVs. <sentence_start/>The incidence of germline findings was slightly higher in patients less than 45 years old compared to patients older than 45 years but did not reach statistical significance (20.7% vs 14.9%, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .443), which is consistent with other studies.<citation rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33106540" doi="10.1038/s41598-020-75062-0" pmcid="PMC7589488" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>CRC in EOC tended to be more frequently left sided (75.9% vs 69.4%), particularly rectal cancers (55.2% vs 40.5%), however, without reaching statistical significance (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .354). <sentence_start/>Somatic findings were less likely to be identified in EOC, consistent with other studies, suggesting that different treatment strategies based only on age in CRC are not justified due to any clear genomic differences when compared to sporadic CRC with average age of onset.<citation rid="bib29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34405229" doi="10.1093/jnci/djab124" pmcid="PMC8634406" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation>

Active smoking was statistically related to MSI-H and <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> mutations. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with data on lung cancer, where <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> mutations are related to smoking status.<citation rid="bib30" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22969966" doi="10.3892/etm.2012.500" pmcid="PMC3438531" count="1"><sup>30</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Correlations with MSI-H and <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> mutations are well known, and studies combining immunotherapy with <italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic> inhibitors, in patients with metastatic CRC, are underway.<citation rid="bib31" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37815847" doi="10.2217/fon-2022-1249" pmcid="PMC12510239" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>MSI-H and TMB-H were statistically significant associated with ESC. <sentence_start/>This information today is very important considering that immunotherapy is being evaluated in the adjuvant setting in trials like ATOMIC.<citation rid="bib32" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation>

The utility of paired GGT and CGP testing was high (≈70%). <sentence_start/>Among EOC patients, 70.0% had only somatic Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants, and among ESC patients, 72.4% had only somatic Tier 1 or Tier 2 variants. <sentence_start/>Overall, the impact of somatic testing in paired GGT and CGP was higher than GGT alone, in terms of detecting actionability. <sentence_start/>However, GGT alone increased utility in detection of genomic alterations in 2.9% in ESC and 6.9% in EOC, warranting further investigation in larger cohorts with different populations to understand broadly the impact of those findings in early cancer detection and CRC prevention.

The median overall survival and recurrence-free survival was not associated with germline or somatic findings; however, these findings should be taken with caution considering that precision medicine in CRC is in constant evolution. <sentence_start/>Since these data were collected, BRAF inhibitors, immunotherapy, and KRAS inhibitors were incorporated into the treatment landscape of advanced CRC.<citation rid="bib33" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39874977" doi="10.1016/S0140-6736(24)02848-4" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="bib34" ref-type="bibr" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="bib35" ref-type="bibr" pmid="40444708" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2501912" pmcid="PMC12197837" count="1">35</citation> Approximately, only 10% of patients were negative for variants of established or potential clinical significance.

The pathway and mutational signature analysis revealed key findings, highlighting frequent somatic mutations in DNA repair and cell cycle pathways. <sentence_start/>Notably, the double strand break response (especially HRR) and TP53 DNA damage pathways showed significant enrichment of alterations. <sentence_start/>Oncogenic signaling in rat sarcoma virus/rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma and PI3K pathways was also commonly altered. <sentence_start/>However, no pathway enrichment differences were observed between early and late disease onset. <sentence_start/>Co-occurrence of mutations in 20 genes was identified, including novel relationships like <italic toggle="yes">ATM-B2M</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH6-B2M</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">RNF43-CDK12</italic>, while no mutually exclusive mutations were found. <sentence_start/>Mutational signature analysis revealed 3 primary signatures implicating alterations in these pathways as driving mutations in CRC: POLE, dMMR, and HRD. <sentence_start/>These pathways are known as key drivers of CRC when altered and have emerging or established implications for prognosis and therapy. <sentence_start/>Oncogenic <italic combination with ipilimumab has been approved by the FDA for patients with dMMR metastatic CRC that have progressed or is unresectable. <sentence_start/>Identifying alterations or mutational Mutational signature analysis additionally detected mutational signature SBS26 in 8 patients without dMMR variant alterations, as well as 1 patient with SBS3 in a patient without mutations in the HRD pathway identified by sequencing. <sentence_start/>SBS26 is 1 of seven mutational signatures associated with dMMR and MSI, while Signature SBS3 is strongly associated with germline and somatic <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> mutations as well as <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> promoter methylation in breast, pancreatic, and ovarian cancers. <sentence_start/>Potentially, these patients may be affected by a genomic alteration out of scope of this assay, such as epigenetic silencing by promoter methylation or may have had loss of heterozygosity of an HRD or MMR gene. <sentence_start/>These findings highlight the importance of mutational signature analysis which could help to identify additional patients eligible for targeted treatments. <sentence_start/>Additionally, some patients showed MMR variants without the dMMR mutational signature, with high TMB in 63.6% of those cases, indicating that these patients may benefit from immunotherapy. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the lack of dMMR mutational signature in this subset of patients does indicate that the mutational signature analysis may be prone to false negatives.

As for some limitations of the study, the cohort composition, the overall patients’ characteristics seen at the multiple Mayo Clinic sites that participated in this study may not mirror those in all regions of the country limiting generalizability. <sentence_start/>Sample size is relatively small, furthermore, lack of long-term follow-up to address the real impact in the cancer-mortality and morbidity associated with systemic treatments, personalized interventions or surgeries related to the findings.

This research has also strengths. <sentence_start/>This is a multicenter, prospective, universal paired genetic testing study. <sentence_start/>Recruitment occurred regardless of stage or family history of cancer. <sentence_start/>This study represents one of the most comprehensive universal genomic analyses performed in a prospective multicentered cohort of unselected patients with CRC and suggests the power of the combination of variant assessment and mutational signatures analysis for identifying the full spectrum of patients that may benefit from therapies targeting the dMMR and HRD pathways and for immunotherapy.
Conclusion

Combined GGT-CGP increases clinical utility for patients with CRC, and these data suggest combined GGT-CGP should be considered for all patients with CRC and may be considered for broader patient populations. <sentence_start/>For patients with EOC experiencing poorer outcomes, there is a higher likelihood of actionability with paired testing. <sentence_start/>CGP-GGT also drives germline resolution for tumor mutations in hereditary cancer genes, expediting clinical recommendations.
